questions.q: What is the electron configuration of Fe (Z = 26)?
questions.why: 26 electrons: [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶.

questions.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of oxygen lower than that of nitrogen?
o: The paired electrons in oxygen's 2p orbital repel each other
Oxygen's electron is in a higher shell
questions.why: Spin-pair repulsion in one 2p orbital makes that electron easier to remove.

questions.q: Which particle has 10 electrons and 11 protons?
questions.why: Sodium (Z = 11) that has lost one electron.

questions.q: Why does first ionisation energy generally increase across a period?
o: Shielding stays the same and nuclear charge increases
Nuclear charge increases, shielding is similar, so the outer electron is attracted more strongly
Electrons are added to new shells
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many said shielding 'remains constant'; examiners wanted similar shielding with greater nuclear charge and smaller radius.

questions.q: What is the full electronic configuration of Cu²⁺?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): answers often kept the 4s electrons. Transition metal ions lose 4s electrons first.

questions.q: Why does successive ionisation energy increase for every element?
o: Nuclear charge increases with each electron removed
Electrons are removed from increasingly positive ions with less electron–electron shielding
The number of protons in the nucleus increases
The principal quantum number of outer electrons increases
questions.why: The proton count stays constant while the electron cloud contracts, increasing electrostatic attraction per remaining electron.

long.q: Explain why the first ionisation energy of aluminium is lower than that of magnesium, and why that of sulfur is lower than that of phosphorus.
scheme: B1: Al's outer electron is in a 3p orbital, Mg's in 3s
B1: 3p is higher in energy / further from the nucleus / shielded by the 3s electrons, so easier to remove
B1: in S the electron removed is from a 3p orbital that holds a pair of electrons
B1: spin-pair repulsion makes it easier to remove

questions.q: How many molecules are in 0.25 mol of CO₂? (L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
A compound is 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass. What is its empirical formula?
What is the percentage yield if 8.0 g is made and 10.0 g was expected?
5.00 g of calcium carbonate (Mr 100) is completely decomposed by heating: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. What volume of CO₂ is produced at room temperature and pressure? (molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹)
questions.why: n(CaCO₃) = 5.00 ÷ 100 = 0.0500 mol, which gives 0.0500 mol CO₂ (1 : 1). Volume = 0.0500 × 24.0 = 1.20 dm³.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of aqueous NaOH is exactly neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄. What is the concentration of the NaOH?
questions.why: n(H₂SO₄) = 0.0200 × 0.150 = 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol; 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, so n(NaOH) = 6.00 × 10⁻³ mol and c = 6.00 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.240 mol dm⁻³. Forgetting the 2 : 1 ratio gives 0.120.

long.q: 0.212 g of an anhydrous carbonate, M₂CO₃, reacts exactly with 20.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. Calculate the relative atomic mass of M and identify M.
scheme: M1: M₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2MCl + H₂O + CO₂ (ratio 1 : 2)

questions.q: What is the shape of an ammonia molecule?
questions.why: Three bonding pairs and one lone pair: pyramidal, bond angle about 107°.

questions.q: What is the bond angle in methane?
questions.why: Four bonding pairs repel equally: tetrahedral, 109.5°.

questions.q: Why does water have an unusually high boiling point for its size?
questions.why: O–H…O hydrogen bonds are much stronger than other intermolecular forces.

questions.q: Which molecule is non-polar overall even though it has polar bonds?
questions.why: CO₂ is linear; the two bond dipoles cancel.

questions.q: Why does magnesium have a high melting point?
o: Strong metallic bonding: attraction between a lattice of positive ions and delocalised electrons
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some described the bonding in magnesium as ionic, and many omitted that the lattice is giant.

questions.q: What is the molecular geometry of sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆)?
questions.why: Six bonding pairs and zero lone pairs around the central sulfur atom repel equally into an octahedral arrangement.

long.q: Explain why water (Mr 18) has a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulfide (Mr 34).
scheme: B1: water forms hydrogen bonds between molecules
B1: because O is much more electronegative than S (O–H strongly polar, lone pairs on O)
B1: hydrogen bonds need more energy to overcome than the van der Waals forces between H₂S molecules

questions.q: Real gases behave most like ideal gases at…
questions.why: Molecules are far apart and fast, so their volume and attractions matter less.

questions.q: Using pV = nRT, what are the units of V?
questions.why: With p in Pa and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, V must be in m³.

questions.q: Which assumption is made in the kinetic theory of an ideal gas?
o: The molecules take up a significant volume
There are no intermolecular forces between the molecules
The molecules are stationary between collisions
questions.why: Real gases behave least ideally at high pressure and low temperature, when these assumptions fail.

questions.q: 0.0200 mol of an ideal gas at 27 °C occupies 500 cm³. What is its pressure? (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
questions.why: Use SI units: T = 300 K and V = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³, so p = nRT/V = (0.0200 × 8.31 × 300) ÷ 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ = 9.97 × 10⁴ Pa. The other answers come from using dm³, cm³ or °C.

questions.q: Iodine is a soft solid that sublimes on gentle warming, but silicon(IV) oxide melts at about 1700 °C. Which statement explains the difference?
o: The I–I covalent bond is weaker than the Si–O bond, so I₂ molecules break apart on warming
Iodine is a simple molecular lattice held by weak instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces; SiO₂ is a giant covalent lattice of strong Si–O bonds
Iodine is ionic and silicon(IV) oxide is covalent
SiO₂ molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds
questions.why: Subliming iodine only overcomes weak forces between I₂ molecules (the I–I bonds stay intact); melting SiO₂ requires breaking many strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice.

questions.q: Hess's law is based on conservation of…
questions.why: The enthalpy change is independent of the route taken.

questions.q: 50.0 g of water rises by 6.0 °C. How much energy was transferred? (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Standard enthalpy change of combustion is always…
questions.why: Combustion releases energy, so it is exothermic.

questions.q: Which is the correct definition of standard enthalpy change of neutralisation?
o: The energy needed to neutralise an acid
The enthalpy change when one mole of acid reacts with one mole of base
The heat released when an acid is diluted
The enthalpy change when one mole of water is formed by an acid reacting with a base under standard conditions
questions.why: Examiners (2023): 'one mole of acid reacting with one mole of base' was a common inadequate answer, and some thought neutralisation needs energy.

questions.q: What is the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation between strong monoprotic acids and strong bases?
questions.why: Strong acids and bases dissociate completely, so the reaction is always H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), yielding about −57 kJ mol⁻¹.

long.q: Use these standard enthalpy changes of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹) to calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation of propane, C₃H₈: C(s) −394, H₂(g) −286, C₃H₈(g) −2219.
scheme: M1: a correct Hess cycle or ΔHf = Σ ΔHc(reactants) − ΔHc(propane)

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of Mn in KMnO₄?
questions.why: K +1, four O −2 each: Mn = +7.

questions.q: In Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, what is oxidised?
questions.why: Br⁻ loses electrons (oxidation number −1 → 0).

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of chromium in Cr₂O₇²⁻?
Cold dilute NaOH reacts with chlorine: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O. What happens to the chlorine?
o: It is only reduced, from 0 to −1
It is only oxidised, from 0 to +1
It is both oxidised to +1 and reduced to −1 (disproportionation)
Its oxidation number does not change
questions.why: One Cl atom goes from 0 to −1 in NaCl and the other from 0 to +1 in NaClO, so the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.

questions.q: In acidic solution, MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺ while Fe²⁺ is oxidised to Fe³⁺. In the balanced equation, how many Fe²⁺ ions react with each MnO₄⁻ ion?
questions.why: Mn changes from +7 to +2, gaining 5 electrons; each Fe²⁺ loses only 1 electron, so 5 Fe²⁺ are needed: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5Fe³⁺.

questions.q: Adding a catalyst to an equilibrium…
o: makes equilibrium reached faster but doesn't move it
questions.why: A catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally.

questions.q: For an exothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature makes Kc…
questions.why: The equilibrium shifts to the endothermic (reverse) direction, so Kc falls.

questions.q: A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a…
questions.why: Acids donate H⁺; bases accept them.

questions.q: How does adding a catalyst affect the equilibrium constant Kc of a reversible reaction?
o: Kc increases because activation energy is lowered
Kc decreases because reactants are consumed faster
Kc is unchanged because forward and reverse rates increase equally
questions.why: A catalyst speeds up both forward and backward reactions by the same factor without altering the thermodynamic equilibrium position.

questions.q: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), what are the units of Kc?
questions.why: Kc = [NH₃]² ÷ ([N₂][H₂]³), so the units are (mol dm⁻³)² ÷ (mol dm⁻³)⁴ = (mol dm⁻³)⁻² = mol⁻² dm⁶.

long.q: 0.50 mol of H₂ and 0.50 mol of I₂ are heated in a sealed 1.00 dm³ flask until equilibrium: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). At equilibrium there are 0.78 mol of HI. Calculate Kc.
scheme: M1: H₂ and I₂ used = 0.39 mol each
M1: at equilibrium [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.11 mol dm⁻³
A1: Kc = 50 (no units)

questions.q: On a Boltzmann distribution, raising the temperature…
o: moves the peak left and up
moves the peak right and down, with more molecules above Ea
reduces the area under the curve
questions.why: More molecules have energy at or above the activation energy; the total area stays the same.

questions.q: A catalyst works by…
o: providing an alternative route with a lower activation energy
questions.why: More particles then have enough energy to react.

questions.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of reaction?
o: It increases the number of collisions
It increases the kinetic energy of the particles
It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful
It shifts the equilibrium to the right
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many said a catalyst increases the number of collisions rather than the frequency of successful collisions.

questions.q: For a first-order reaction with respect to reactant A, what is the effect on rate of tripling the concentration of A?
o: The rate increases by a factor of 9
questions.why: Rate = k[A]¹; doubling or tripling [A] changes the rate by that exact multiple for a first-order reaction.

questions.q: Marble chips react with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. Which change would NOT increase the initial rate of reaction?
o: Using powdered marble instead of chips
Using the same mass of marble as larger chips
Using acid of double the concentration
questions.why: Larger chips have a smaller total surface area, so there are fewer collisions per second between acid particles and the solid, and the rate decreases.

long.q: Use the Boltzmann distribution to explain why a small rise in temperature greatly increases the rate of a reaction.
scheme: B1: at higher temperature the curve shifts right / lower peak, area unchanged
B1: many more molecules have energy ≥ Ea
B1: so more frequent successful collisions per second (frequency of collisions rises only slightly)

questions.q: Across Period 3, atomic radius…
questions.why: Nuclear charge rises with similar shielding, pulling the electrons closer.

questions.q: Which Period 3 oxide is amphoteric?
questions.why: Al₂O₃ reacts with both acids and bases.

questions.q: Why does atomic radius decrease across Period 3?
o: Electrons are added to new shells
Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays similar
questions.why: Examiners (2023): say 'similar shielding', and link more protons to stronger attraction.

questions.q: Which Period 3 chloride dissolves in water to give a neutral solution of about pH 7?
questions.why: Ionic NaCl simply dissolves; AlCl₃ gives an acidic solution and the covalent chlorides SiCl₄ and PCl₅ are hydrolysed to give HCl (pH 1–2).

questions.q: Why is the melting point of silicon much higher than that of phosphorus?
o: Silicon atoms are smaller than phosphorus atoms
Silicon has metallic bonding with delocalised electrons
Phosphorus has fewer protons in its nucleus
Silicon is a giant covalent lattice, whereas phosphorus is made of P₄ molecules held by weak instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces
questions.why: Melting silicon breaks many strong covalent bonds; melting phosphorus only overcomes weak intermolecular forces between P₄ molecules.

questions.q: Down Group 2, the solubility of the hydroxides…
questions.why: Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble; Ba(OH)₂ is much more soluble.

questions.q: Down Group 2, the thermal stability of the carbonates…
questions.why: Larger cations polarise the carbonate ion less, so it is harder to decompose.

questions.q: How does the solubility of the Group 2 hydroxides change down the group?
questions.why: Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble; Ba(OH)₂ is much more soluble. (Group 2 sulfates show the opposite trend.)

questions.q: Which equation shows the reaction of magnesium with steam?
questions.why: With steam magnesium forms its oxide and hydrogen; Mg(OH)₂ forms in the very slow reaction with cold water, and magnesium is +2, never +1.

questions.q: Why does the reactivity of the Group 2 metals with water increase down the group?
o: The nuclear charge decreases down the group
The sum of the first and second ionisation energies decreases, so M²⁺ ions form more easily
questions.why: Down the group the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so less energy is needed to remove two electrons, even though nuclear charge increases.

questions.q: Concentrated H₂SO₄ is added to solid NaBr. Which is produced?
o: HBr and some Br₂ and SO₂
questions.why: Bromide is a strong enough reducing agent to reduce some of the sulfuric acid to SO₂.

questions.q: Silver nitrate gives a cream precipitate soluble in concentrated ammonia. Which halide?
questions.why: AgCl is white (dissolves in dilute NH₃), AgBr cream (concentrated), AgI yellow (insoluble).

questions.q: Which reagent is used to test for halide ions (X⁻), as opposed to a halogen (X₂)?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some used iodine where iodide was meant: be precise about halogens (X₂) and halides (X⁻). Halide ions are tested with aqueous silver nitrate.

questions.q: Chlorine water is added to colourless aqueous potassium iodide. What is observed?
o: No change, because chlorine is less reactive than iodine
The solution turns brown as iodine forms
questions.why: Chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂, and aqueous iodine is brown.

questions.q: Why does the volatility of the halogens decrease from chlorine to iodine?
o: The molecules have more electrons, so instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces between them are stronger
The X–X covalent bond becomes stronger
Hydrogen bonding increases down the group
questions.why: Boiling a halogen only overcomes intermolecular forces; larger molecules with more electrons have stronger id–id forces, so more energy is needed.

questions.q: Why is N₂ unreactive?
o: Its triple bond is very strong
questions.why: N≡N has a high bond energy.

questions.q: Which pollutant forms when nitrogen and oxygen react in a hot engine?
questions.why: High temperatures let N₂ and O₂ combine to form nitrogen oxides.

questions.q: Why is nitrogen gas very unreactive?
o: The N≡N triple bond has a very high bond energy
questions.why: A lot of energy is needed to break the triple bond, and the molecule is non-polar.

questions.q: In polluted air, NO₂ helps convert SO₂ into SO₃: SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO, then NO + ½O₂ → NO₂. What is the role of NO₂?
o: It is a reducing agent that is used up
It is a catalyst: it oxidises SO₂ and is then regenerated
It is a product of acid rain
It reacts with SO₂ to form sulfuric acid directly
questions.why: NO₂ takes part in the first step and is reformed in the second, so it is not used up overall: it acts as a catalyst for the oxidation of SO₂.

questions.q: Which test confirms that a solid contains ammonium ions?
o: Add dilute HCl; a gas turns limewater milky
Add aqueous silver nitrate; a white precipitate forms
Warm with aqueous NaOH; a gas turns damp red litmus blue
Add acidified barium chloride; a white precipitate forms
questions.why: OH⁻ removes a proton from NH₄⁺: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O, and ammonia is the only common alkaline gas.

questions.q: Structural isomers have the same…
questions.why: Same molecular formula, different structures.

questions.q: Why can but-2-ene show cis/trans (E/Z) isomerism?
o: There is restricted rotation about C=C with two different groups on each carbon
questions.why: Both conditions are needed for geometrical isomers.

questions.q: A chiral carbon has…
questions.why: It gives non-superimposable mirror images (optical isomers).

questions.q: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₄H₉Br?
questions.why: 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane: two chain arrangements, each with two different positions for Br.

questions.q: The C–Br bond in bromoethane breaks heterolytically. Which pair of species forms?
questions.why: In heterolytic fission one atom keeps both bonding electrons; the more electronegative bromine takes them, giving a carbocation and a bromide ion. Homolytic fission gives the radicals.

questions.q: Alkanes react with chlorine in UV light by…
questions.why: UV splits Cl₂ into radicals: initiation, propagation, termination.

questions.q: Ethene reacts with bromine by…
questions.why: The electron-rich C=C attacks the polarised Br₂.

questions.q: What is the mechanism when ethene reacts with hydrogen bromide?
questions.why: The electron-rich C=C attracts the δ+ hydrogen of HBr: an electrophile adds across the double bond.

questions.q: Which is a propagation step in the reaction of methane with chlorine in UV light?
questions.why: A propagation step uses one radical and produces another, so the chain continues; the first option is initiation and the two radical–radical combinations are termination.

questions.q: But-2-ene is heated with concentrated acidified potassium manganate(VII). What is the organic product?
questions.why: Hot concentrated KMnO₄ splits the C=C bond. Each CH₃CH= end becomes CH₃COOH, so CH₃CH=CHCH₃ gives two molecules of ethanoic acid. The diol forms with cold, dilute KMnO₄.

long.q: But-1-ene reacts with hydrogen bromide to give two products. Name the major product and explain why it is formed in the larger amount.
scheme: B1: 2-bromobutane
B1: via the secondary carbocation (CH₃CH⁺CH₂CH₃)
B1: which is more stable than the primary one, because alkyl groups push electrons towards (are electron-donating to) the positive carbon

questions.q: Which halogenoalkane hydrolyses fastest?
questions.why: The C–I bond is the weakest, so it breaks most easily.

questions.q: Heating a halogenoalkane with ethanolic KOH mainly gives…
questions.why: In ethanol, OH⁻ acts as a base and removes HX.

questions.q: Which reagents and conditions convert a halogenoalkane into a nitrile?
o: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some gave the conditions for carbonyl → hydroxynitrile instead of halogenoalkane → nitrile.

questions.q: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is hydrolysed by aqueous hydroxide ions by the SN1 mechanism. What is the first step?
o: OH⁻ attacks the carbon as the C–Br bond breaks, in one step
OH⁻ removes a hydrogen atom to form an alkene
The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically to form a tertiary carbocation and Br⁻
questions.why: In SN1 the slow first step is ionisation to a carbocation, which is stabilised by three alkyl groups; OH⁻ then attacks the carbocation. The one-step attack describes SN2.

questions.q: 1-chlorobutane is warmed with aqueous NaOH, then dilute nitric acid and aqueous silver nitrate are added. What is seen?
questions.why: Hydrolysis releases Cl⁻ ions, which give white AgCl. Nitric acid is added first to neutralise excess OH⁻, which would otherwise precipitate silver oxide.

questions.q: Which alcohol is NOT oxidised by acidified dichromate(VI)?
questions.why: Tertiary alcohols have no H on the carbon bearing the OH.

questions.q: Distilling a primary alcohol with acidified dichromate as it forms gives…
questions.why: Distilling removes the aldehyde before it oxidises further; heating under reflux gives the acid.

questions.q: Which alcohol is not oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?
questions.why: Tertiary alcohols have no H on the C–OH carbon, so the orange dichromate stays orange.

questions.q: Which alcohol gives a yellow precipitate when warmed with alkaline aqueous iodine?
questions.why: The tri-iodomethane (CHI₃) test is positive for alcohols containing the CH₃CH(OH)– group; propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, has it, the others do not.

questions.q: Which reagent and conditions convert ethanol into ethene?
o: Pass the vapour over heated Al₂O₃
questions.why: Ethene forms by dehydration, which needs a heated Al₂O₃ catalyst (or hot concentrated H₂SO₄/H₃PO₄). Steam with H₃PO₄ is the reverse reaction, hydration of ethene.

long.q: Describe how you could use acidified potassium dichromate(VI) and one other reagent to distinguish between propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
scheme: B1: warm each with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇: propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol turn it orange to green
B1: 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary) leaves it orange
B1: distil off the product: propan-1-ol gives an aldehyde, propan-2-ol a ketone
B1: Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with the aldehyde only (or Fehling's: red precipitate)

questions.q: Which reagent distinguishes an aldehyde from a ketone?
questions.why: Aldehydes give a silver mirror; ketones don't. 2,4-DNPH reacts with both.

questions.q: NaBH₄ reduces a ketone to…
questions.why: Ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols.

questions.q: What is the product when propanone is reduced with NaBH₄?
questions.why: Ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols.

questions.q: Which reagent gives an orange precipitate with both aldehydes and ketones?
questions.why: 2,4-DNPH reacts with any C=O group in an aldehyde or ketone; the other three are oxidising agents that react only with aldehydes.

questions.q: Ethanal reacts with HCN in the presence of a little KCN. What are the mechanism and the product?
questions.why: CN⁻ attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon and the intermediate is then protonated, giving CH₃CH(OH)CN: the OH and CN are on the same carbon, C-2 of the three-carbon chain.

questions.q: An alcohol and a carboxylic acid with a concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst form…
questions.why: Esterification (a condensation reaction).

questions.q: Carboxylic acids react with sodium carbonate to give…
questions.why: They are acidic enough to release CO₂ from carbonates.

questions.q: Ethanoic acid is warmed with ethanol and a little concentrated sulfuric acid. What forms?
questions.why: This is esterification; the acid is a catalyst and the reaction is reversible.

questions.q: Which reagent reduces ethanoic acid to ethanol?
o: H₂ with a nickel catalyst at room temperature
questions.why: Carboxylic acids need the powerful reducing agent LiAlH₄; NaBH₄ reduces aldehydes and ketones but not carboxylic acids, and dichromate is an oxidising agent.

questions.q: Ethyl propanoate is heated under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide. What are the products?
questions.why: Alkaline hydrolysis of CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃ gives the alcohol and the carboxylate salt (not the free acid). The acid part of the ester is propanoate; the alcohol part is ethanol.

questions.q: A nitrile is hydrolysed by heating with dilute acid. It forms…
questions.why: R–C≡N + 2H₂O + H⁺ → RCOOH + NH₄⁺.

questions.q: Reacting a halogenoalkane with KCN in ethanol…
o: lengthens the carbon chain by one
questions.why: CN⁻ substitutes for the halogen, adding a carbon.

questions.q: How is a primary amine made from a halogenoalkane?
o: Heat with excess ethanolic ammonia in a sealed tube
React with hydrogen and a nickel catalyst
questions.why: Excess ammonia reduces further substitution to secondary and tertiary amines.

questions.q: Which reagent converts propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN, into propylamine, CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂?
questions.why: The C≡N group is reduced to –CH₂NH₂ by H₂/Ni (or LiAlH₄). Heating with dilute acid hydrolyses the nitrile to a carboxylic acid instead.

questions.q: Why is excess ammonia used when making ethylamine from bromoethane?
o: To stop the bromoethane being hydrolysed to ethanol
To make it less likely that the ethylamine formed reacts further with bromoethane
questions.why: Ethylamine is itself a nucleophile and can attack more bromoethane to give secondary and tertiary amines; a large excess of NH₃ makes ammonia the most likely nucleophile.

questions.q: What is the repeat unit of poly(propene)?
questions.why: Opening propene's C=C gives –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–.

questions.q: Why are poly(alkenes) hard to dispose of?
questions.why: Strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds; burning them can release toxic gases.

questions.q: Why are addition polymers like poly(ethene) hard to dispose of?
o: They are non-biodegradable because of strong non-polar C–C and C–H bonds
questions.why: Burning them can release toxic gases.

questions.q: Which monomer forms the addition polymer with repeat unit –CH₂–CHCl–?
questions.why: Addition polymers form from alkenes; CH₂=CHCl (chloroethene) opens its C=C bond to give –CH₂–CHCl– (PVC). Chloroethane has no C=C bond.

questions.q: Why can burning waste poly(chloroethene) (PVC) be hazardous?
o: It produces toxic, acidic hydrogen chloride gas
It produces only carbon dioxide and water
It explodes because it contains oxygen
questions.why: The chlorine in the polymer ends up as HCl (and other toxic chlorinated compounds) when PVC is burned.

questions.q: To go from ethanol to ethanoic acid, use…
questions.why: Full oxidation of a primary alcohol under reflux.

questions.q: Which reaction adds one carbon atom to a carbon chain?
questions.why: The nitrile formed can then be hydrolysed or reduced.

questions.q: Which conditions convert a nitrile into a carboxylic acid?
o: Heat under reflux with dilute acid
questions.why: Acid hydrolysis turns –C≡N into –COOH; reduction would give an amine.

questions.q: Which two-step route converts propene into propanone?
o: Step 1: steam with H₃PO₄ catalyst; step 2: heat with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇
Step 1: H₂ with Ni; step 2: acidified K₂Cr₂O₇
Step 1: steam with H₃PO₄ catalyst; step 2: NaBH₄
questions.why: Hydration of propene gives mainly propan-2-ol (via the more stable secondary carbocation), and oxidising a secondary alcohol gives the ketone. NaBH₄ is a reducing agent.

questions.q: Compound X decolourises bromine water and gives effervescence with aqueous sodium carbonate. Which could X be?
questions.why: Decolourising bromine water shows a C=C bond, and effervescence (CO₂) with Na₂CO₃ shows a carboxylic acid; only propenoic acid has both.

questions.q: A broad IR absorption at 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ with a peak near 1700 cm⁻¹ suggests…
questions.why: Broad O–H (acid) plus C=O.

questions.q: In a mass spectrum, the M⁺ peak gives the…
questions.why: The molecular ion peak is at the Mr (the M+1 peak hints at the carbon count).

questions.q: What causes the small M+1 peak in a mass spectrum?
questions.why: About 1.1% of carbon is ¹³C, so the M+1 height helps count the carbon atoms.

questions.q: A compound shows a strong infrared absorption near 1715 cm⁻¹, sharp C–H absorptions near 2900 cm⁻¹, and no broad absorption anywhere between 2500 and 3600 cm⁻¹. Which compound could it be?
questions.why: The 1715 cm⁻¹ peak is C=O; the absence of any broad O–H absorption rules out alcohols and carboxylic acids.

questions.q: The mass spectrum of a bromoalkane shows molecular ion peaks at m/e 122 and 124. What are their approximate relative heights?
questions.why: Bromine has two isotopes, ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br, in roughly equal amounts, so a molecule with one Br gives M and M+2 peaks of about equal height. 3 : 1 is the pattern for one chlorine atom.

questions.q: A reaction is feasible when ΔG is…
questions.why: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS ≤ 0 for a feasible reaction.

questions.q: Lattice energy becomes more exothermic when ions are…
questions.why: Smaller, more highly charged ions attract more strongly.

questions.q: Which change has a positive entropy change?
o: A solid dissolving to make aqueous ions
questions.why: Particles become more disordered (more ways to arrange energy).

questions.q: For CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Above what temperature is the reaction feasible?
questions.why: Feasible when ΔG = ΔH − TΔS ≤ 0, so T ≥ ΔH/ΔS = 178 000 J mol⁻¹ ÷ 161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 1106 K. Not converting kJ to J gives 1.11 K.

questions.q: The lattice energy of NaCl is −787 kJ mol⁻¹. The enthalpy changes of hydration are Na⁺ −406 kJ mol⁻¹ and Cl⁻ −378 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the enthalpy change of solution of NaCl?
questions.why: ΔHsol = −(lattice energy) + ΣΔHhyd = +787 + (−406 − 378) = +3 kJ mol⁻¹: breaking the lattice needs slightly more energy than hydration releases.

long.q: Use the following data (kJ mol⁻¹) to calculate the lattice energy of sodium chloride: ΔHf NaCl −411; atomisation Na +107; first IE Na +496; atomisation Cl +122; first electron affinity Cl −349.
scheme: M1: a correct Born–Haber cycle

questions.q: Cu²⁺/Cu E° = +0.34 V and Zn²⁺/Zn E° = −0.76 V. What is the cell e.m.f.?
questions.why: E°cell = E°(positive) − E°(negative) = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V.

questions.q: How much charge passes when 0.20 A flows for 965 s? (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹)
o: Both: 193 C, which is 0.0020 mol of electrons
questions.why: Q = It = 193 C; 193 ÷ 96 500 = 0.0020 mol of electrons.

questions.q: Standard electrode potentials are measured against which reference?
questions.why: Standard conditions: 298 K, 100 kPa, 1.00 mol dm⁻³ solutions; the hydrogen electrode is defined as 0.00 V.

questions.q: What is true when a chemical electrochemical cell reaches equilibrium?
o: The standard electrode potential E° becomes 0 V
The cell potential E_cell becomes 0 V
questions.why: At equilibrium, the driving force (Gibbs free energy change ΔG) is zero, so the operating cell voltage drops to zero.

questions.q: For Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s), E° = +0.34 V. What is the electrode potential at 298 K when [Cu²⁺] = 0.010 mol dm⁻³? (E = E° + (0.059/z) log[oxidised form])
questions.why: E = 0.34 + (0.059 ÷ 2) × log 0.010 = 0.34 + 0.0295 × (−2) = +0.28 V. Lowering [Cu²⁺] makes the potential less positive; forgetting z = 2 gives +0.22 V.

long.q: Use E° values (Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77 V; Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V) to calculate E°cell and predict whether Fe³⁺ ions oxidise copper.
scheme: B1: positive, so the reaction 2Fe³⁺ + Cu → 2Fe²⁺ + Cu²⁺ is feasible

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.010 mol dm⁻³ HCl?
A buffer resists pH change because…
o: it contains a weak acid and its conjugate base that remove added H⁺ or OH⁻
questions.why: Large reservoirs of HA and A⁻ absorb small additions.

questions.q: Ka for a weak acid is 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. What is its pKa?
questions.why: pKa = −log Ka = 5.

questions.q: What is the pH of an equimolar buffer solution containing ethanoic acid (pKa = 4.76) and sodium ethanoate?
questions.why: By the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]). When [salt] = [acid], log(1) = 0 so pH = pKa.

questions.q: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), the equilibrium mixture at a total pressure of 200 kPa has a mole fraction of NO₂ of 0.40. What is Kp?
questions.why: p(NO₂) = 0.40 × 200 = 80 kPa and p(N₂O₄) = 0.60 × 200 = 120 kPa, so Kp = p(NO₂)² ÷ p(N₂O₄) = 6400 ÷ 120 = 53.3 kPa.

long.q: Calculate the pH of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³).

questions.q: Doubling [A] quadruples the rate. The order with respect to A is…
questions.why: rate ∝ [A]ⁿ and 2ⁿ = 4, so n = 2.

questions.q: The half-life of a first-order reaction…
questions.why: First-order half-lives are independent of concentration.

questions.q: Rate = k[A]²[B], with concentrations in mol dm⁻³ and time in s. What are the units of k?
questions.why: Overall order 3: k = rate ÷ (mol dm⁻³)³.

questions.q: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 20 s. What fraction of the reactant remains after 60 s?
questions.why: 60 s is three half-lives, and each one halves the amount: ½ × ½ × ½ = 1/8.

questions.q: The hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane by OH⁻ has the rate equation rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr]. What does this suggest about the mechanism?
o: OH⁻ is not involved in the reaction at all
The reaction happens in a single step involving both reactants
The rate-determining step involves only (CH₃)₃CBr, and OH⁻ reacts in a later, faster step
questions.why: Only species in or before the rate-determining step appear in the rate equation. Zero order in OH⁻ means it reacts after the slow step (ionisation to a carbocation), consistent with SN1.

long.q: For the reaction A + B → C, doubling [A] doubles the rate and doubling [B] quadruples the rate. Write the rate equation and give the units of k when concentrations are in mol dm⁻³ and the rate in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
scheme: B1: first order in A, second order in B
B1: rate = k[A][B]²
A1: units dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹

questions.q: Down Group 2, the solubility of the sulfates…
questions.why: Hydration enthalpy falls faster than lattice energy as the cation gets bigger.

questions.q: How does the thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates change down the group?
questions.why: Higher temperatures are needed to decompose carbonates further down the group.

questions.q: Why do Group 2 carbonates become more thermally stable down the group?
o: Larger cations have lower charge density and polarise the carbonate ion less
Lattice energy increases down the group
questions.why: Less distortion of the carbonate's electron cloud means it breaks up less easily.

questions.q: Why does the solubility of the Group 2 sulfates decrease down the group?
o: The lattice energy becomes much more exothermic down the group
The enthalpy change of hydration of M²⁺ becomes less exothermic, while the lattice energy changes much less
Sulfate ions become larger down the group
The sulfates become more covalent down the group
questions.why: The large sulfate ion dominates the lattice, so lattice energy falls only slightly as M²⁺ grows; hydration enthalpy falls more, so ΔHsol becomes more endothermic.

questions.q: What are the products when calcium nitrate is heated strongly?
questions.why: Group 2 nitrates decompose to the oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen: 2Ca(NO₃)₂ → 2CaO + 4NO₂ + O₂. Forming the nitrite and oxygen is typical of Group 1 nitrates.

questions.q: Why are transition metal compounds often coloured?
o: d-orbitals split in a ligand field and electrons absorb visible light moving between them
questions.why: The light not absorbed gives the complementary colour.

questions.q: What is the coordination number of [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
questions.why: Six water ligands form dative bonds to Cu²⁺.

questions.q: Which is a bidentate ligand?
questions.why: en forms two dative bonds through its two nitrogen atoms.

questions.q: Why do transition metal complexes exhibit distinct colours in aqueous solution?
o: d-orbitals split in energy and d-electrons absorb specific frequencies of visible light
Transitions occur between s and p orbitals
Electrons emit light during nuclear decay
questions.why: Ligand field splitting causes d-d electronic transitions; the absorbed photons promote electrons, leaving the complementary colour visible.

questions.q: Concentrated HCl is added to pink aqueous cobalt(II) ions: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O. Which describes the change?
o: Blue to pink; the coordination number stays at 6
Pink to blue; octahedral (6-coordinate) to tetrahedral (4-coordinate)
Pink to blue; the oxidation state of cobalt changes from +2 to +4
Pink to green; octahedral to square planar
questions.why: This is ligand exchange: the larger Cl⁻ ligands replace water, and only four fit around Co²⁺, giving a blue tetrahedral complex. Cobalt stays +2 (6 × 0 → 4 × −1 with overall charge 2+ → 2−).

long.q: Explain why aqueous copper(II) ions are coloured.
scheme: B1: ligands split the 3d orbitals into two energy levels
B1: a d electron absorbs light of a particular frequency to move to the higher level
B1: the complementary colour is seen (blue)
B1: Cu²⁺ has a partly filled 3d subshell (3d⁹)

topics.name: Introduction to A Level organic chemistry

questions.q: Benzene's bond lengths are all equal because…
o: its π electrons are delocalised over the ring
questions.why: Delocalisation gives six identical C–C bonds between single and double.

questions.q: Molecules that are non-superimposable mirror images show which isomerism?
questions.why: They rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions.

questions.q: A chiral centre is a carbon atom that is:
o: bonded to four different atoms or groups
part of a C=C double bond
questions.why: Four different groups make two mirror-image arrangements possible.

questions.q: Which of these compounds contains a chiral centre?
questions.why: C-2 of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid carries four different groups (CH₃, H, OH, COOH). In propan-2-ol the central carbon has two identical CH₃ groups.

questions.q: A chemist makes a chiral compound as a racemic mixture. How does this sample affect plane-polarised light?
o: No net rotation, because equal amounts of each enantiomer rotate the plane equally in opposite directions
questions.why: A racemic mixture contains 50% of each enantiomer; their opposite rotations cancel, so the mixture is optically inactive.

questions.q: Benzene reacts with bromine in the presence of FeBr₃ by…
questions.why: Substitution keeps the stable delocalised ring.

questions.q: What is the electrophile in the nitration of benzene?
questions.why: Concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ form the nitronium ion NO₂⁺.

questions.q: How does benzene react with bromine in the presence of FeBr₃?
questions.why: Substitution keeps the stable delocalised ring; FeBr₃ makes the Br⁺ electrophile.

questions.q: Methylbenzene is heated under reflux with alkaline KMnO₄, then the mixture is acidified. What is the organic product?
questions.why: Hot KMnO₄ oxidises the alkyl side chain to –COOH while the stable aromatic ring is left intact.

questions.q: Methylbenzene reacts with chlorine in UV light with no catalyst. Where does substitution happen?
o: On the ring, mainly at the 2- and 4-positions
Chlorine atoms add across the ring's double bonds
Nowhere: no reaction occurs without a halogen carrier
On the methyl group, by free-radical substitution, giving C₆H₅CH₂Cl
questions.why: UV light produces Cl• radicals, which substitute H atoms on the alkyl side chain. Ring substitution at the 2- and 4-positions needs a halogen carrier such as AlCl₃.

long.q: Explain why benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition with bromine, and name the catalyst used.
scheme: B1: delocalised π electrons give extra stability
B1: substitution keeps the delocalised ring; addition would destroy it
B1: catalyst FeBr₃ (or AlBr₃ / iron)

questions.q: Why is chlorobenzene much less reactive to nucleophiles than chloroalkanes?
o: The C–Cl bond is strengthened by overlap with the ring's π system
questions.why: Partial double-bond character makes the C–Cl bond harder to break.

questions.q: Why is chlorobenzene much less reactive towards nucleophiles than chloroethane?
o: Chlorine is more electronegative in benzene
A chlorine lone pair overlaps with the ring's π system, strengthening the C–Cl bond
questions.why: The partial double-bond character makes the C–Cl bond harder to break.

questions.q: Which halogenoalkane is hydrolysed fastest?
questions.why: The C–I bond is the weakest, so it breaks most easily.

questions.q: Which reagents and conditions convert benzene into chlorobenzene?
o: Cl₂ with an AlCl₃ catalyst at room temperature
questions.why: The halogen carrier AlCl₃ (or FeCl₃) polarises Cl₂ to make the Cl⁺ electrophile for electrophilic substitution; benzene does not react with HCl.

questions.q: Chlorobenzene and 1-chlorobutane are each warmed with aqueous NaOH, then acidified with dilute HNO₃ and aqueous AgNO₃ added. What is seen?
o: A white precipitate only with chlorobenzene
questions.why: Only 1-chlorobutane is hydrolysed to release Cl⁻; the C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene is strengthened by overlap with the ring, so no Cl⁻ forms.

questions.q: Phenol reacts with bromine water to give…
questions.why: The OH group activates the ring, so substitution happens readily without a catalyst.

questions.q: Which is the strongest acid?
questions.why: Order: ethanoic acid > phenol > water > ethanol.

questions.q: Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol?
o: The phenoxide ion's negative charge is delocalised into the ring
questions.why: A more stable anion means the O–H proton is lost more readily.

questions.q: Which of these does phenol react with: sodium metal, aqueous NaOH, aqueous Na₂CO₃?
questions.why: Phenol is acidic enough to react with Na and NaOH, but it is too weak an acid to release CO₂ from carbonate, unlike carboxylic acids.

questions.q: Why does phenol react with bromine water at room temperature with no catalyst, while benzene needs a halogen carrier?
o: Phenol is a stronger acid than benzene
The OH group makes phenol more soluble in water
Bromine water is a stronger electrophile than Br₂ alone
A lone pair on the oxygen is delocalised into the ring, raising its electron density so it attacks the electrophile more readily
questions.why: The increased electron density of the ring in phenol can polarise Br₂ itself, so substitution (at the 2-, 4- and 6-positions) happens readily without a catalyst.

questions.q: Acyl chlorides react with water to give…
questions.why: Vigorous hydrolysis with steamy HCl fumes.

questions.q: What forms when ethanoyl chloride reacts with water?
questions.why: Acyl chlorides hydrolyse rapidly at room temperature, giving steamy HCl fumes.

questions.q: Which is the strongest acid?
questions.why: Electron-withdrawing chlorine atoms stabilise the carboxylate ion.

questions.q: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with ethylamine. What is the organic product?
questions.why: In nucleophilic addition–elimination, the amine's lone pair attacks the carbonyl carbon and HCl is lost, giving a substituted (N-ethyl) amide.

questions.q: Why is ethanoyl chloride, not ethanoic acid, used to make the ester phenyl ethanoate from phenol?
o: Ethanoic acid is too strong an acid
Phenol reacts with ethanoic acid to give a salt instead
Phenol is a poor nucleophile, so it reacts with the more reactive acyl chloride but not readily with a carboxylic acid
Ethanoyl chloride acts as a catalyst
questions.why: The phenol O lone pair is partly delocalised into the ring, making phenol a weak nucleophile; the carbonyl carbon of an acyl chloride, bonded to both O and Cl, is much more δ+ than in a carboxylic acid.

questions.q: Why is phenylamine a weaker base than ethylamine?
o: The lone pair on N is delocalised into the ring, so it's less available
questions.why: Delocalisation reduces the lone pair's ability to accept a proton.

questions.q: Amino acids exist in solution near neutral pH as…
questions.why: The –COOH loses H⁺ and the –NH₂ gains it.

questions.q: Why is phenylamine a weaker base than ammonia?
o: The ring donates electrons to nitrogen
The nitrogen lone pair is partly delocalised into the benzene ring
questions.why: The lone pair is less available to accept a proton.

questions.q: Which reagents and conditions convert phenylamine into benzenediazonium chloride?
o: NaNO₂ and dilute HCl, heated under reflux
Sn and concentrated HCl, then NaOH
questions.why: Nitrous acid is made in situ from NaNO₂ and HCl; the temperature is kept below 10 °C because the diazonium ion decomposes to phenol and N₂ when warmed.

questions.q: In which form does the amino acid glycine mainly exist in a solution of pH 1?
questions.why: In strong acid both groups are protonated: the –NH₂ gains H⁺ and the –COO⁻ of the zwitterion is protonated to –COOH, so the ion carries an overall +1 charge.

questions.q: A polyester is formed from…
o: a diol and a dicarboxylic acid
questions.why: Ester links form, eliminating water each time (condensation polymerisation).

questions.q: Which pair of monomers forms a polyester?
o: A diol and a dicarboxylic acid
A diamine and a dicarboxylic acid
An amino acid and an alkene
questions.why: Each ester link forms with loss of water; a diamine and a diacid would make a polyamide.

questions.q: Which linkage is found in a polyamide?
questions.why: Nylon and proteins both contain the amide (peptide) link.

questions.q: Nylon-6,6 can be made from hexanedioyl dichloride, ClOC(CH₂)₄COCl, and hexane-1,6-diamine. Which small molecule is eliminated?
questions.why: Each amide link forms from –COCl and –NH₂, losing HCl. Water is lost when the dicarboxylic acid is used instead of the diacyl dichloride.

questions.q: Why can polyesters and polyamides be broken down more easily than poly(alkenes)?
o: They have weaker C–C bonds in the chain
Their ester and amide links can be hydrolysed by acids, alkalis or enzymes
questions.why: Hydrolysis breaks the polar –COO– or –CONH– links back into monomers; poly(alkenes) have only non-polar C–C and C–H bonds and no such reactive link.

questions.q: Which reagent converts a carboxylic acid to an acyl chloride?
questions.why: SOCl₂ (or PCl₅) replaces OH with Cl.

questions.q: How is phenylamine made from benzene?
o: Nitrate with conc. HNO₃ and H₂SO₄, then reduce with Sn and conc. HCl
questions.why: Nitration gives nitrobenzene; reduction gives phenylamine (freed with NaOH).

questions.q: Which reagent converts a carboxylic acid into an acyl chloride?
questions.why: PCl₅ or PCl₃ also work; aqueous HCl does not.

questions.q: Which reagent distinguishes phenol from cyclohexanol?
questions.why: Phenol decolourises bromine water and gives a white precipitate; cyclohexanol does not react. Both react with sodium, and neither reacts with Na₂CO₃ or Tollens' reagent.

questions.q: Propanal reacts with HCN (with KCN catalyst). Why is the product obtained as a racemic mixture?
o: The product has no chiral centre
The C=O group is planar, so CN⁻ attacks from either side with equal probability
questions.why: Attack from the two faces of the planar carbonyl gives the two enantiomers of 2-hydroxybutanenitrile in equal amounts, so a single-enantiomer product would need further separation.

questions.q: In proton NMR, a peak split into a triplet has how many H on adjacent carbons?
questions.why: The n + 1 rule: n = 2 gives a triplet.

questions.q: Why is D₂O added in proton NMR?
o: To identify O–H and N–H protons, whose peaks disappear
questions.why: Deuterium exchanges with labile protons, removing their peaks.

questions.q: Why is D₂O added to a sample in proton NMR?
o: It is the reference at 0 ppm
O–H and N–H protons exchange with D, so their peaks disappear
questions.why: Comparing spectra with and without D₂O identifies the O–H or N–H peak.

questions.q: In thin-layer chromatography a spot moves 3.0 cm while the solvent front moves 7.5 cm from the baseline. What is the Rf value?
questions.why: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front = 3.0 ÷ 7.5 = 0.40; Rf is always less than 1.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃?
questions.why: The two CH₃ carbons are in identical environments, and the CH carbon is different, so there are two carbon environments and two peaks.

long.q: A compound has an ¹H NMR spectrum showing a triplet (3H) at δ 1.2 and a quartet (2H) at δ 3.6, and a broad peak that disappears with D₂O. Identify the compound and explain the splitting.
scheme: B1: ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH
B1: the CH₃ triplet is next to a CH₂ (n + 1 = 3)
B1: the CH₂ quartet is next to a CH₃
B1: the O–H peak disappears as H exchanges with D
